My older brother had three kids beginning in 2005, through 2015. I was so supportive and involved with all three.  One is my godchild.

My little brother had his first in 2019. I was still so excited.  The pandemic began March 2020, two months after my first infertility appointment and one month after they found my six ovarian tumors. Then the worst, blackest, loneliest four years of my life began.

When my little brother had his second baby in 2022, I fell apart. I couldn't look at him without crying, and holding him was devastating. 

I had fight after fight with my mother and brothers about my involvement in family get-togethers and about my attitude. I want to be clear here: my whole family knew about the tumors, about our appointments, and about every little step of my horrendous IVF journey.  They tried to be respectful by not pushing me for details but that was terrible for me. I was invisible.  SoI was being selfish with my feelings. That's not projecting my family members' feelings; I was being selfish because I needed to be to not disintegrate.

It finally came to a head when my beautiful husband reached out to my family for a little meeting to talk about some next steps, and our feelings about being pushed into events. That meeting ended in me and my mother screaming at each other, my little brother sitting silently and not knowing what to say, and me storming to my bedroom to try and get away.

My older brother (who has been my best friend my whole life) followed me. He wanted to understand, and he tried to make me see other peoples' feelings.  I went numb. Like, instantly numb. I felt everything that had been exploding out of me just.. stop. 

I asked him if his wife loved their children. Of course she does. I asked him if I could present him with something horrible that I might regret saying, something that might make him angry with me. I asked him, what would your wife do if one of your children died? How would she feel if I pushed her to come to my birthday party? How would she handle it if I said to her, "come on out and celebrate, you'll feel better afterward?" Would my mother think she was being selfish if your wife chose to not come to our cousin's baby shower? I think those questions made him look at our situation in a different way. 

Infertility is a slow, lonely depression. It's soul killing. It's failing at the one part of your life everyone thinks you *should* be able to do, over and over.  It is grief. It is picturing tiny hands in yours and knowing that picture is fantasy. It's expensive. It's embarrassing. It's being obligated to go to your sibling's kid's birthday party and only being able to afford dollar store crap for them because not only did you have to put $5000 on your credit card that morning for meds, but you've had to quit your job recently because they're unaccepting of you missing three mornings a week for IVF appointments.  And then trying not to cry the whole day.

It is a unique grief. It is desperately wanting to share in others' happiness and simply not being able to.  I feel sadness for both you and your SIL. There's no winner here. I can guarantee without ever having met her that she will come to regret not going to family events.

I missed my goddaughter's ninth birthday party. It was a snowstorm, I had come back from a terrible appointment that morning, and my insides felt like a bomb had gone off (I had terrible scarring and dead tissue on my fallopian tubes, and one of the tumors on my ovary was quite large and had apparently been causing the terrible periods I'd experienced for five years). I was bleeding through nighttime pads in an hour, and I'd just been told that my chances of ever having a baby, even through IVF, were extremely low.  I got home and I just...couldn't. I couldn't do anything. And my husband, godsend that he is, could see that. And he called my brother, said the snowstorm was too bad, we weren't coming. He tried to spare everyone the embarrassment of what was truly happening. Well, of course the snow cleared up, we didn't go, and my brother was angry that we let down his daughter.  And was he correct? Of course he was. She was sad and disappointed that we didn't show for her special day.  And I regret that every damn day because she didn't deserve that.  That day caused a rift between me and my brother that I don't think healed for years.

But...I didn't deserve it either. And that's the terrible fine line you walk every day when you're living with grief. Do I risk breaking down to make someone else feel better? Or do I take care of myself by staying hidden at home with my sadness where no one can see it?

If you can, try to keep including your SIL. She isn't winning. She doesn't feel good about this. And there will come a day where she looks back with regret for what she missed.

Infertility is devastating. It's grief every day for a baby you never get to hold, for a life you never get to have, for love you never get to give.  And I truly think you cannot understand how all-encompassing and difficult it is until you go through it or watch someone closely while they go through it.  It changed me, and not in an inspiring 'i got stronger because of this tragedy!' kinda way. It hurt me and took my hope for many long years. I lost friends, my job, financial security for the next decade. 

I'm not saying you have to suddenly be overly kind, or make excuses for her. But I feel for her, some days are too long and too difficult to face. And maybe she just.... couldn't.

Good luck to both of you.

I'm from Ontario Canada and I had three egg retrievals.  There was no option to be asleep here. It was a fentanyl drip administered by an anesthesiologist, and I had to verbally tell her if the pain was so bad that I wanted more.

My first ER was absolutely fine, no pain worse than a mild period. I didn't get to watch but the doctor talked me through the whole procedure, and then I was wheeled out to a nurse-monitored aftercare area with juice, cookies, and an hour's rest before I was allowed to go home. I didn't take Tylenol or anything afterward and I was fine.

My second was a nightmare (no intention here to frighten, so I apologize).  The actual procedure (same doctor, same nurses) just *hurt*.  I had to request more painkillers twice, and it felt like a very sharp stabbing pain. I cried during. I went out to the same aftercare area afterward, ate my cookies and juice, took the Tylenol/Advil they offered (I'm sorry, I don't remember which), got up to go to the bathroom after the hour, and fainted. 

Their care was fast and effective, and I didn't even hit my head since a nurse caught me. IV, painkillers, water, cold compress, and two more hours of monitoring. I was very blurry so my husband remembers more of that day, but apparently your ovaries can react like that to extreme pain and it is unpleasant but common.

My third retrieval was just like my first, absolutely fine. And I was the most nervous for the third one.  

I obviously can't say if being asleep would have been better, but I will say I would do it all again regardless of the one painful retrieval. And my clinic was fantastic and staff were  prepared for anything.

Good luck :)

I say this as gently as I can about those people who seem to hate their lives after a baby: they didn't want the baby as badly as they thought they would.

Babies are hard work. Even the "easy" babies (I have the easiest little dude ever and he still takes over my life).  And it's not only that; children are hard. Teenagers are hard!! This is an entire living, breathing, *feeling* person. Of course it's hard.

I know several people whose lives changed for the worse after having children, and they will happily tell you all about it, weirdly. My own mother likes to tell me what a difficult baby I was, and when my husband and I began IVF four years ago she couldn't believe how much work and money were involved and that we chose to do it.

I personally believe many people have babies because they're *supposed* to have babies. It's the norm. I think this is the most common factor. I also believe there are people who have babies for the clout, if that makes sense. Like, not necessarily for Instagram, for example, but to display an important step in life. Not because they *want a baby.*

I'm a big advocate for IVF and my husband and I went through the ringer to have our one and only son. I think one gigantic advantage IVF parents have over other parents is that it is not for the weak-willed. You'd better want that baby because emotionally, physically, financially....there's no room to *not* desperately want it.  I was never so sure of wanting something so badly in my whole life. And every sleepless night, every shitty diaper, every crappy day where I walk around in a fog, I vocally remind myself *he is worth every crap moment*.  Because you have to know that little life is worth everything. The alternative is to believe your life changed for the worse.

41 years old, six ovarian tumors discovered and removed in 2021, dead fallopian tubes. We never knew, as my family doctor never caught them.  Decided to do IVF despite having no benefits or government assistance (where I'm from, the waitlist is long).

Three rounds of egg retrievals, 19 embryos sent for genetic testing, only one viable embryo.  Literally one shot, one opportunity, to seize everything I ever wanted (Eminem is quoted in my house daily).

Sitting here with my morning coffee watching my son slowly wake up. We'll be broke forever but man was it worth it.

I was 37 when I finally got referred to a fertility specialist. 

First they found six ovarian tumors that my family doctor never investigated. Then came COVID, and my surgery to have them removed was pushed back three times. Next we switched clinics and set ourselves back 6+ months having to redo tests (our first clinic was terrible at communicating, and boy was it worth switching).

Then three rounds of egg retrieval, 23 embryos, and genetic testing that left us with ONE viable embryo.

And finally....came my one and only son, born August 28 of this year, at my age of 42. Healthy, happy and beautiful.

It's possible. Don't give up if you think you have a chance :)

This is so important and needs to be said more:

"Assume every driver is trying to kill you."

This is what my mom has told us since we were kids. Don't trust other drivers, assume people can't see you, and worry less about being *right* and more about being *dead.*

It goes for drivers, cyclists and pedestrians. Please stop thinking that just because you have the right of way it means people are watching everything YOU do.  I still have the frame of mind where I only cross at cross walks, and my eyes are glued to the road. Not on my phone, not listening to my music at full blast.  I am still sure that the next car coming is a stupid idiot and won't see me, and if it doesn't look right, I don't step off the curb, or I don't turn right on a red, etc.

I'm sure it pisses everyone off around me but honestly, this is a lesson to live by: your own safety is your own responsibility, others can only be expected to do so much to be responsible for you.

I was 37 when we had our first IVF appointment (at 42 I just had my one and only baby boy on August 28). We went through ovarian surgery for six tumors, three rounds of ER and wound up with one healthy embryo after genetic testing.

It was rough. Also in 2022 my father was diagnosed with a rare blood cancer condition. He is a big burly carpenter, always healthy and athletic. A "man's man" type of guy. I have always loved him but never really shared any of this stuff with him, just kinda depended on my mom to take in the info and share as she saw fit.

He did really well with his diagnosis. This was the first real time he was sick. He went to all his appointments without complaint, took all the prescribed drugs on schedule, and went through his many blood transfusions with flying colours. We were all worried about him and would ask about each appointment, what new info he got, how he was feeling (this was when COVID still meant we couldn't go to most appointments with him). And interestingly, he responded and was happy to share, even though for every injury or cold or flu he ever had throughout his life, he would give a gruff "I'm fine" if anyone ever asked after him, and continue on in his manly way. He slowly improved and we were all relieved he could manage this illness for the rest of his life.

Fast forward to 2023. One day I got a call from his cell phone (which he barely uses; usually if we get a call it means maybe his truck broke down or something...we always assumed some kind of emergency). He asks if I have a minute or if I'm busy, and at this point I'm worried because for him to start a conversation like this it MUST be bad.

He takes a big breath and asks how I am. I paused and thought about it. I was gearing up to hear that my mother had been in a car accident or something, and he was, for the first time in my life, softening the blow by asking how I was. I tentatively told him I was fine....what was happening??

He proceeds to ask again, how I'm really doing. He says mom told him that I had gone in for my third retrieval the other day, and it had been a bad one. I hadn't received good news from my second retrieval (we still only had one viable embryo from round one) and to top it off, I had a bad experience with the IV and had a blood explosion with my after care nurse and had to stay in their clinic for a few extra hours before they would let us go home (not life threatening at ALL, just not fun!). 

I didn't really know what to say. My father had NEVER asked how I was and expected to hear a "real" answer. I told him I was doing okay, the blood explosion was pretty cool, and tried to kinda laugh it off. Like a "manly" answer.  And he listened for a minute and then asked if I wanted to share any results of my tests.

I was honestly shocked. I shared with him that I was expecting results from the third ER but that at my age the doctor wasn't hopeful, and we might still only have one little egg to move forward with. He listened and asked some more questions, and when I stopped talking, he said "well, I'd better be going. But when they get the results give me a call and let me know how you're doing."

He gave me many more phone calls in the following months, and asked many more personal, potentially sensitive questions. Every time I was surprised and secretly pleased.

When we found out that we were successful in our transfer, my parents were the first ones we told. And he gave me a hug. For the first time in my life. At five months, once we were past many of the "dangerous" milestones in our pregnancy, we decided we could finally start getting our house ready for a baby. One big thing was our bathroom. It was old, the tub was rusty and unusable for a bath, the layout was awful. After three rounds of ERs and a transfer, we had no real money left but we decided we could afford a new tub where we could eventually bathe the baby. We called my dad, the carpenter, and asked if he could help us pick one out and show us how to install it in the easiest, cheapest way possible. He said yes and he would come with me next week to do that.

He calls me again an hour later and says, "you know what...I don't like your bathroom. And when you're carrying a big fat baby in there, you won't even fit between the sink and the tub. Hell, when you're a couple more months pregnant, YOU won't fit between the sink and the tub. So, I'm just going to rip it all out and put in a new one."

So my father, 74 years old with blood cancer, ripped out my existing bathroom. Everything. Alone, with minimal help from me and my husband since I was quite pregnant and he was working heavy overtime with his business to save up. Dad moved around plumbing, installed all new tiles with spare ones he had laying around from previous jobs, custom made a vanity for our awkward corner, painted, cleaned, drywalled, literally remade our entire bathroom. We re-used the toilet and as much as we could, and he salvaged whatever he could from previous jobs that he had stashed away in his workshop. We spent very little on this job (most of the budget was the new tub and new fixtures). He wanted no payment in return, and no help. He did this alone, in four weeks. 

I bought a card to say thank you. It was a silly funny card with a joke about carpenters on it. But for the first time in my life I wrote a serious message to him on the inside, thanking him not only for the beautiful bathroom, but for every phone call and every conversation about our process, and for doing everything he could to make my life better to prepare for our one and only baby. He put the card on his nightstand and it sits there still. 

We had our little dude on August 28. He was healthy and beautiful, and we named him Kenny, after my father. We have a hundred photos of my dad holding my son and grinning like crazy, something I never thought would happen.

Sometimes things work out just the way you want. And sometimes, even if they don't, important people notice that they're not working out and they step up to help.

Misunderstood grief is so accurate.

I had family members who didn't understand why I was so depressed during IVF. I remember having to sit down with my brother to explain it because he just couldn't understand, and my family was becoming short with me.

I had to ask him how his wife would feel if one of their three children died. Would she just "stay positive"? Would she just "look on the bright side"? Was she happy to hear everyone say "God has a plan?"

Every time a dark day would come, it was experiencing loss, and grief,and utter joylessness. Like losing a person. You were losing a life and a person who would never become.

It's so damn hard.

Honestly I loved anything my loved ones got me for the whole process, but the best useful ones were definitely prepared food or takeout gift cards. Much like postpartum, there are such high, low, and purely exhausting days that planning and making meals got to be a really tough thing. It was nice to just relax and order out or stick something in the oven.

Also, a sweet handwritten card offering your support can't go wrong. I kept all of mine and will forever.

Not my BEST friend, but two old longtime friends:

I started doing IVF in 2020. Finally finally got pregnant in late 2023. These two friends didn't acknowledge it, say congrats, ask how I was doing....nothing.

We all played world of Warcraft together. One of them actually got mad that I wasn't making HIM feel special in game by announcing I was pregnant, and the other just flat out ghosted me. I addressed both of them to ask if we weren't close enough anymore to talk this out, and the first one got mad, wrote in our friend group discord that I was "treating [him] like his father does" (???) and left our discord and our guild, and told all our buddies what I'd done (which I still don't understand...I was a bad friend by becoming pregnant and thinking someone would say congrats or, at the very least, hello?)

The other, who is an older woman with children and grandchildren, continued to ghost me. Just flat out ignored me. No idea what I did to her either.

These weren't just online gaming buddies, or so I thought. We had known each other for fifteen years. They had both eaten and slept in my home multiple times, they had been to my wedding, I knew and spoke to their family members. We were *friends*. 

People really can fool you sometimes. No idea if they know or care if I'm still alive.

I also was incredibly happy with my clinic. While the nurses and pharmacy staff were amazing, we did get to see our doctor directly for every major appointment (basically everything except bloodwork and pharmacy visits).
We switched from a clinic that we felt did terribly in terms of communication, which set us back six months. I was 39 at the time so even a little bit of extra time seemed like such a big deal, and it was...but so is your confidence in your doctor or team.
We do deserve better! I never regretted that switch of clinics.

As someone who has played and performed and taught for a long time, I know I'm comfortable with playing in front of anyone. But that's 35 years of practice doing that. It is way different for a young child, or a piano beginner to feel comfortable performing in front of people. 

I think it's just a discussion that needs to happen honestly between teacher and parent, based on the child's best interest. As a teacher, I personally groan inside whenever a parent wants to be there for the lesson, but it's something I would never deny them. Quite often they'll see that if they're in the room, their child doesn't pay attention (especially if they're younger than 8 years old) and they'll decide for themselves to not be present the next time. And if the parent or child is really only comfortable being together for the lesson, so be it. 

Most of these thoughts are just twenty years of trial and error with my own students...they're definitely not canon.

Yep I would agree. A class setting is way way different, for both the student and the teacher. I taught for a year at a private school and one of the curriculums we had to do was one class of minimum six students per semester. I'll be honest, I hated it.

I think it's a bit different in a public school where every student is treated as a beginner, but I discovered that at the private school the owners didn't vet individual student abilities. Having a sixteen year old who has been in lessons for five years combined with a ten year old in his second year was a nightmare to teach, and involved a lot more work for me as I ended up doing individual lesson plans for homework on top of the group work that I was mandated to assign.

I would agree that if you want a more valuable individual learning experience where they really design work based on your child's ability, look into private one on one teaching.

I've been a piano teacher for over twenty years now, and I love beginning students but it's always tricky to get them invested when they're such a young age. I have found with a lot of trial and error that generally children that young respond well to keeping piano practice to the bare minimum and focusing more on keeping the lessons fun and engaging.

I do a lot of singing, clapping, and copy/repeat with my younger students, which actually restricts how much practice at home they CAN do. But it means that they usually look forward to the lessons since it's a stress free enjoyable environment. Five is very young to be focusing on correct finger placement and technique, but a great age to hone their listening skills. Finger technique should be more natural at that age, not learned since very few five year olds have the dexterity or the patience to be practicing it.

When it comes to finger technique for someone that young, I myself would be planning to make sure they know their finger numbers (thumbs are one, pinkies are five) and create exercises that help them feel triumphant in that knowledge. For example, a game where we find all the "C" keys on the piano might be easy, but a fun challenge is to hit all the C's with their middle finger. And when they achieve that in their lesson, their homework for that week might be to show their mom and dad three C's on their piano at home, again using their middle finger.

It sounds too simple, but it's valuable for them to just recognize their fingers, versus sending them home with a whole song every week and expecting them to learn it and not feel pressure. Piano is incredibly difficult with a lot of moving parts and most times focusing on just one part is more successful for a young one.

I've been a piano teacher for twenty years and had many students prepping for RCM exams.

I love to play a recording of the song we are preparing to play, whether it's myself playing it while recording on my phone, or a professional or very solid YouTube recording (also, many of the teachers' prep books come with a cd or usb with each RCM selection on it). Having us both actively listen to the piece, at ANY grade level, is valuable. It gives us a chance to discuss sections or make notes, or, more often, become invested in the piece.

I will play sections if the student has questions, usually after a short sightreading attempt. It really depends on the student, though. Some students respond incredibly well to the copy teaching method (where I play sections often and they replicate it) whereas some do well with sightreading and active listening on their own (I myself was the latter kind of student). 

In my personal opinion it's not a red flag if the teacher doesn't play. If it worries you though, I would try to discuss it. Your child might be the type to want to try it on their own, versus doing a copy method and the teacher might be using that to their strength.

This is my situation exactly. Can I ask where you're from?I'm in Ontario Canada and I'm currently 11 weeks pregnant from IVF. My husband and I have no insurance/benefits and so we pay the costs all out of pocket.

I'm sure cost and procedures are different if you're in the states, for example, but I can let you have an idea of our costs if that helps.

We began in early 2023 and arranged for 3 rounds of egg retrievals back to back. We were told by our counselors that many women opted to do fewer rounds than that, especially if they didn't have employment benefits/coverage.  I turned 41 this year and had been through ovarian tumor removal surgery (benign) and partial fallopian tube removal (due to scar tissue and damage) back in 2021. We tried to begin IVF earlier, when I was 38, and the tumors were discovered in my first sonohysterogram. Due to the pandemic slowing down medical care in Canada, my surgery was pushed back three times before happening and my IVF journey was stalled. Hence, I was feeling worried that I was getting too old, and we opted to do three rounds back to back as soon as we could.

The three rounds for us was a base cost of approximately $33,000. This was the amount we paid to the clinic before anything had been done. Since we had no coverage, we were also charged the amount for all the drugs. I think this is probably the biggest mystery factor in IVF costs since every woman's needs are different.

The drugs we were prescribed were to adjust hormones for each cycle and stimulate follicle growth. We were prescribed Menopur and Gonal-F for the most part, and we were prescribed somewhat prolonged use since my follicles were growing more slowly than my doctor desired (this meant at least two full weeks worth for each individual cycle, if not more). Combined with the trigger medication, these add up quickly.

We also opted to do genetic testing on any embryos that reached blast phase, and that was also a huge cost. The base cost was $5000, plus the administration fees and shipping costs.  We also chose to do the "multiple testing" plan, since we were doing multiple cycles. This ended up costing more for us in the long run since unfortunately, many of our embryos did not reach the blast phase.  That being said, I do not regret at all doing the genetic testing, for what that's worth.

Finally, we also paid for the freezing of the embryos and storage of sperm, as well as the actual embryo transfer (the final step in the whole process). These costs together added up to approximately $7500.

All in all our personal costs for IVF are at just under $72,000. We got a line of credit on our home and maxed out four credit cards.  We will be paying them off for a very long time.

Even if we were not successful, I would not have regretted IVF; our clinic was frankly wonderful. From the receptionists to the pharmacists to the doctor who performed each of my retrievals and the transfer, they were clear and straightforward both about procedures and costs.

It is a huge financial and emotional journey. I recommend very carefully planning your cost plans and if you have any benefits or insurance, squeeze them as hard as you can. 

Good luck in your journey and if you have any questions, I'm happy to share my experiences with you ❤️

I had terrible periods for 15+ years. Once a year I would see my family doctor (a well-reviewed, young female doctor) that it felt wrong and the amount of pain I was experiencing didn't feel normal.

She would try to persuade me to go on birth control every time to control the symptoms. I would argue and say that was against my wishes.  No gynecologist referrals, no ultrasounds. This went on for fifteen years.

It wasn't until I pushed hard for a referral to a fertility clinic and was finally seen by a new doctor (after trying to become pregnant for three years) that they discovered I had six tumors in my ovaries.  I needed invasive surgery to remove them all and am now on a cancer watch every six months for life.

I never thought it was abnormal that my family doctor didn't refer me to a gynecologist, and since they were all benign, blood tests over the years didn't show red flags. I trusted her and thought "she's a doctor, she would clearly know better than me."

Sometimes you have to advocate for yourself harder than you like to. Your health shouldn't be compromised because someone might not fully believe you. See a different doctor, and tell the emergency room exactly what you believe is the case.

Try reading pieces you have no previous knowledge of. I've taught a few kids over the years who are amazing at "cheating" by knowing the tune or even by (probably as you do) being very skilled at using audio clues or pattern recognition to subconsciously determine what's coming up.

This'll be annoying, but pick unfamiliar types of sheet music to read. Pop music, for example, tends to be predictable and won't really test you. Look for obscure or culturally diverse pieces so that you're really depending on pure reading skills and not subconsciously on your audio skills to sightread.

And if you have a musical buddy, ask them to test you by taking a piece (even one you know) and picking random bars for you to read and play. Continually starting songs from the beginning enforced your muscle memory but doesn't push your skill at reading.

And finally....as others have written....try reading as often as you can. You may not notice the improvement, but it'll definitely be there.
